# Plots and tables {#sec-plots}

The package produces the paper's figures and tables directly from its own output: estimate tables
from `sc_estimate()`, fitted laws from `sc_fitted_law()`, and posterior summaries from
`sc_posterior()`. Because the plotting functions use base graphics, several calls can be combined
into one figure with `layout()` or `par(mfrow = )`. Each returns the data it drew, invisibly, so
you can check what is on the page.

The examples below use the toy fit of @sec-quantities and run in seconds, though their estimates
mean nothing.

```{r}
#| label: p-setup
library(sconjoint)
toy <- sc_load(system.file("extdata", "toy_fit.rds", package = "sconjoint"))
f <- paste0("tax", 1:6, "_linear")            # the linear term of each bracket's rate
bn <- c("Below $10k", "$10-35k", "$35-85k", "$85-175k", "$175-375k", "Above $375k")
dem <- function(g) g$party == "Dem"
means <- sc_estimate(toy, lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_mean(bn[j], f[j])))
means_dem <- sc_estimate(toy, lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_mean(bn[j], f[j], w = dem)))
shares <- sc_estimate(toy, lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_share(bn[j], f[j])), bounded = FALSE)
laws <- lapply(f, function(cc) sc_fitted_law(toy, cc))
```

## Estimates

`sc_plot_estimates()` takes one or more estimate tables and draws one row per target: a point for
the estimate and a line for its 95% interval, leaving the point hollow when its interval is missing.
Passing several tables as named arguments separates them into groups in different colors and places
those names in the legend; calling `plot()` on an estimate table invokes the same function.

Several arguments adjust the display: `labels` and `order` control the rows, `scale = 100` expresses
values in percent, and `xlim` sets the horizontal limits. In addition, `reference` adds comparison
values such as true values in a simulation or regression AMCEs, while `hide_wide` drops intervals
that span almost all of $[0, 1]$. `groups` names groups of rows, such as the levels of one
attribute, in grey at the left, with a small gap between groups; `sc_plot_laws()` and
`sc_plot_preferences()` take it too.

```{r}
#| label: p-estimates
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.6
sc_plot_estimates(All = means, Democrats = means_dem)
```

@fig-sim-estimates compares estimates with the truth, while @fig-gs-compensation and
@fig-br-party-shares show three groups.

## Fitted laws

`sc_plot_laws()` draws the fitted laws returned by `sc_fitted_law()` in either of two layouts. Under
the default `layout = "ridges"`, the laws share one panel and one axis, arranged one row each and
scaled to the same height. There `groups` names groups of rows, `height` above about 1 lets each
ridge rise over the row above it, and `outline = "line"` joins the bin midpoints instead of drawing
steps. Under `layout = "panels"`, each law gets its own panel. In both layouts `means` adds the
corrected means: as a vertical line in a ridge, and as a red line with its 95% interval as a red
bar in a panel. In a simulation, true density functions can be passed through `truth`.

Because the curves show fitted values before the one-step correction, a corrected mean need not sit
at a curve's center. In the toy fit, the corrected means lie far from the curves, so the examples
below leave them out.

```{r}
#| label: p-laws-ridges
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
sc_plot_laws(laws, labels = bn, groups = rep(c("Lower brackets", "Upper brackets"), each = 3),
             height = 1.3, bins = 300, outline = "line")
```

```{r}
#| label: p-laws
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.8
sc_plot_laws(laws[c(1, 6)], labels = bn[c(1, 6)], layout = "panels", ncol = 2)
```

@fig-gs-distributions and @fig-br-distributions draw ridges with means, and @fig-sim-laws uses
panels with the truth.

## Summary figure

`sc_plot_preferences()` draws the paper's summary figure with one row per feature across aligned
panels: (A) the mean taste, (B) its fitted law as a ridge, (C) the share with a positive taste, in
percent, and, when `ames` is supplied, (D) the choice effect in percentage points, with optional
`reference` values shown as grey diamonds.

Row order is set with `order`, while per-panel options---`xlim`, `ticks`, and `titles`---are each
supplied as a list named by panel. In Panel C, `hide_wide` hides intervals that span at least 95
points.

```{r}
#| label: p-preferences
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 2.6
sc_plot_preferences(means, laws, shares, order = bn[c(1, 2, 6)])
```

@fig-gs-preferences and @fig-br-preferences are full examples.

## Shares favoring and opposing

`sc_plot_shares()` shows a table of `sc_share()` estimates as two bars per row: a blue bar to the
right for the percent of respondents whose taste for the contrast is positive, and a red bar to the
left for the rest. The dark line at the end of the blue bar is the share's 95% interval, which
`intervals = FALSE` leaves out and `hide_wide` drops when it spans at least 95 points. Like the
other plots, it takes `labels`, `order` and `groups`. The bars need shares between 0 and 1, so the
shares come from the bounded update (`sc_estimate()`'s default), not from `bounded = FALSE` as in
the setup above.

```{r}
#| label: p-shares
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
shares_b <- sc_estimate(toy, lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_share(bn[j], f[j])))
sc_plot_shares(shares_b, groups = rep(c("Lower brackets", "Upper brackets"), each = 3))
```

Panel C of the summary figure shows the same shares as points with intervals, which is easier to
read when the intervals matter.

## Importance

`sc_plot_importance()` draws importance shares as horizontal bars in percent, with each bar's value
printed at its end. Each group is passed as a named argument holding an estimate table of
`sc_importance()` targets, and target names such as `"All.low"` lose their common prefix so that
rows from different tables match by attribute. In addition, `combine` adds attributes into display
groups.

```{r}
#| label: p-importance
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
fn <- toy$data$data$feature_names
g <- list(low = fn[1:4], middle = fn[5:8], high = fn[9:12], revenue = fn[13:16])
imp_all <- sc_estimate(toy, sc_importance(g, names = paste("All", names(g), sep = ".")),
                       bounded = FALSE)
imp_dem <- sc_estimate(toy, sc_importance(g, w = dem, names = paste("Dem", names(g), sep = ".")),
                       bounded = FALSE)
sc_plot_importance(All = imp_all, Democrats = imp_dem,
                   combine = list(rates = c("low", "middle", "high"), revenue = "revenue"))
```

@fig-gs-importance is the full example.

## Lines

`sc_plot_lines()` plots estimates against an ordered setting `x`, such as an income bracket, drawing
a line with points for each estimate table and a shaded band for its 95% intervals. Each table has
one row per value of `x`; an axis label via `xlab` is required, and `hline` sets the dashed
reference line (defaulting to 0.5 for probabilities and shares).

Because one call draws a single panel, multi-panel figures are built by setting up `layout()`,
calling the function once per panel with `legend = FALSE`, and drawing one legend.

```{r}
#| label: p-lines
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
sc_plot_lines(All = means, Democrats = means_dem, x = 1:6,
              xlab = "Income bracket (lowest to highest)")
```

@fig-gs-contests has three panels.

## Respondents

`sc_plot_posterior()` draws posterior summaries from `sc_posterior()`, with `which` picking the
contrast. Its plot depends on whether `truth` is supplied: without `truth`, it shows respondents
sorted by posterior mean with each respondent's 95% posterior interval; with `truth` in a
simulation, it plots each posterior mean against the true value, adding a 45-degree line and the
correlation.

```{r}
#| label: p-posterior
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.4
post <- sc_posterior(toy, contrasts = c(tax6_linear = 1), nodes = 256)
sc_plot_posterior(post, ylab = "Posterior taste for a higher top rate")
```

@fig-sim-posterior uses `truth`.

## Adjusting a figure

`sc_plot_estimates()` takes `labels`, `order`, `xlim`, `xlab` and `main`, and `colors`, one color
per table; the other plot functions take most of the same arguments (see their help pages). The
first example relabels the rows, reverses their order and changes the two colors.

```{r}
#| label: p-custom-rows
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.6
sc_plot_estimates(All = means, Democrats = means_dem, order = rev(bn),
                  labels = setNames(paste("Bracket", 1:6), bn), colors = c("#333333", "#BD4C39"))
```

The second fixes the horizontal axis, its label and a title. With `scale = 100`, values and limits
are in percent.

```{r}
#| label: p-custom-axis
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.4
sc_plot_estimates(means, xlim = c(-30, 30), xlab = "Mean taste for the linear rate term (logit units)",
                  main = "Toy fit")
```

The single-panel plots (`sc_plot_estimates()`, `sc_plot_laws()` with `layout = "ridges"`,
`sc_plot_shares()`, `sc_plot_importance()`, `sc_plot_lines()` and `sc_plot_posterior()`) can share
one figure through `layout()` or `par(mfrow = )`. `sc_plot_preferences()` and the `"panels"` layout
of `sc_plot_laws()` use the whole page and cannot.

```{r}
#| label: p-custom-layout
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.4
layout(matrix(1:2, 1), widths = c(1, 1.2))
sc_plot_estimates(means, main = "Mean utility")
sc_plot_laws(laws, labels = bn, height = 1.3, bins = 300, outline = "line", main = "Fitted laws")
layout(1)
```

## Tables

`sc_table()` places one or more estimate tables side by side, with one row per target and one column
per table. Each cell holds the estimate alongside either its 95% interval (`style = "ci"`) or its
standard error in parentheses (`style = "se"`), while `n = TRUE` adds the number of respondents. The
output can be returned as a data frame, a Markdown table, or a LaTeX `tabular`.

```{r}
#| label: p-table
sc_table(All = means, Democrats = means_dem, digits = 3, n = TRUE)
```

In a Quarto or R Markdown chunk with `#| results: asis`, `format = "markdown"` prints the result as
a table:

```{r}
#| label: p-table-md
#| results: asis
sc_table(All = means, Democrats = means_dem, digits = 3, format = "markdown")
```

For a paper, `format = "latex"` returns a booktabs table. It escapes `%`, `&`, `_`, `#`, and `$` in
labels and headers, while other LaTeX special characters, such as `~` or `^`, must be written in
LaTeX directly.

```{r}
#| label: p-table-tex
sc_table(All = means, Democrats = means_dem, labels = paste("Bracket", 1:6), style = "se",
         format = "latex", caption = "Toy estimates")
```

@sec-gs and @sec-br each show one table at full scale.
